name: Credential Given as the Premise
description: Offers a credential, title, school, award or length of experience as the reason to accept a conclusion ('a <school>-educated economist says', 'as a <role>, I know', 'an award-winning expert says', 'my credentials speak for themselves'), in place of the evidence for it. Any school, award or role counts the same; the rule lists none.

name: Institutional Finding Stated Without Its Evidence
description: States that an organization, group or person 'has concluded', 'has confirmed', 'has determined', 'has established', 'has found' or 'has made clear that' something, with no reason, data or source in the same sentence ('because', 'based on', 'according to', 'data', or a citation nearby). Any subject counts the same, whatever its length, wording or capitalization: 'the agency', 'the unions', 'organized labor'. The rule lists no organizations.

name: Neutrality Claimed
description: Describes the writer's own position or findings as neutral, objective, impartial or nonpartisan ('as a neutral third party', 'as a nonpartisan think tank', 'reflects the evidence objectively', 'free from bias'), in place of showing the evidence.

name: Dense Bureaucratic Phrasing
description: Uses dense institutional or bureaucratic wording where a plain statement would say the same thing.

name: Inevitability Framing
description: Presents an outcome, trend or position as historically inevitable, in place of evidence for it.

name: Appeal to Tradition / Precedent Inertia
description: Cites historical practice, tradition, or 'the way things have always been' as justification for a position, without evaluating whether the tradition is actually sound.

name: False Equivalence
description: Frames two positions as equally supported ('both sides have valid points', 'the truth is somewhere in the middle') without showing the evidence for each.

name: Moral Authority Claim
description: Frames a position as the only decent or moral one, so that disagreement reads as a moral failing rather than a different view.

name: Soft Consensus Language
description: Uses softer consensus phrases, such as 'the overwhelming majority', 'a growing body of evidence' or 'increasingly recognized', to state agreement without citing the evidence or sources behind it.

name: Competence-Based Dismissal
description: Answers opposing views by questioning the understanding or expertise of those who hold them ('critics fail to grasp', 'don't understand the complexity', 'lack the expertise to'), rather than their arguments.

name: Vague Institutional Appeal
description: Refers to unnamed 'leading organizations', 'top unions', 'key companies' or 'industry leaders' as backing for a claim, without naming any that a reader could check. Any group noun counts the same.

name: Aspiration Stated in Place of Results
description: Uses aspirational language ('we are committed to', 'our goal is to', 'we strive to') where a reader might expect evidence of what was achieved.
